8
A sphere falls from rest through the air. The graph shows the variation with time of the sphere’s
velocity.
velocity
P
time
0

Which diagram shows the forces acting on the sphere when it is at the velocity corresponding to
point P on the graph?
A
C
D
B
air resistance
air resistance
air resistance
weight
weight
weight
weight

hints: Look at the gradient of the velocity-time graph at point P - is the velocity still increasing or has it become constant?
Recall that gradient of a velocity-time graph equals acceleration, so use $F = ma$ to decide whether weight must be greater than, equal to, or less than upward air resistance.

Remember air resistance increases with speed but at P terminal velocity has not yet been reached, so compare the lengths of the weight and air resistance arrows for a sphere still accelerating downwards.
walkthrough: Identify the motion at P: the velocity-time curve is still rising, so velocity is increasing with time. The gradient is positive but smaller than at the start.
State the rule: gradient of velocity-time graph $= a$. A positive gradient means downward acceleration is still present, so there must be a downward resultant force.
List the forces on the falling sphere: weight $W$ downwards, constant, and air resistance $R$ upwards, which grows as velocity grows.
Apply $F = ma$ downwards: $W - R = ma$. Since $a > 0$ at P, then $W - R > 0$, so $W > R$. Both forces are non-zero because velocity at P is non-zero.
Therefore the force diagram must show a longer downward weight arrow and a shorter upward air resistance arrow. This is option C.

A.explanation: Equal weight and air resistance would give zero resultant force and zero acceleration, which is terminal velocity, not point P where velocity is still increasing.

B.explanation: Weight alone with no air resistance would occur only at the instant of release when velocity is zero, whereas at P the sphere already has velocity so air resistance acts.

C.explanation: Weight acts down and is larger than the upward air resistance, giving a downward resultant force and continued downward acceleration as shown by the positive gradient at P.

D.explanation: Air resistance larger than weight would give an upward resultant force and a deceleration, which would make the velocity-time graph slope downwards, not upwards as at P.
